summary: This work shows that distributed quantum computing with one high-coherence nuclear-spin data qubit per node can achieve fault-tolerant quantum error correction by exploiting biased noise on photon-generated Bell pairs. The key insight is that phase errors on Bell pairs can be engineered to appear solely as measurement errors suppressible by repetition, while bit-flip errors propagate to data qubits where they are corrected by the code itself, eliminating the need for distillation ancillas.
motivation: Distributed quantum computing architectures interconnect small nodes via optical links, but face a critical asymmetry: in-node operations are high-fidelity while inter-node photonic communication is noisy and relies on low-coherence electron spins. Previous schemes required multiple ancilla qubits per node for Bell-pair and GHZ-state distillation, which is impractical since most platforms provide only one or two controllable nuclear spins per node.
method: The authors engineer a communication error bias where photonic Bell pairs suffer frequent phase errors ($p_z \approx 10\%$) but rare bit-flip errors. They design syndrome-extraction circuits so that phase noise flips measurement outcomes without propagating to data qubits, allowing simple measurement repetition to suppress these errors. For Floquet codes, only one data qubit per node is needed; for stabilizer codes like the surface code, one ancilla qubit enables weight-four parity measurements via GHZ states generated from Bell pairs.
result: Floquet codes (honeycomb and hyperbolic) achieve $p_z$ thresholds of approximately $0.88\%$ and $0.74\%$ respectively with $p_{\text{res}} = 10^{-3}$ residual noise. Surface code memory reaches a $p_z \approx 4.5\%$ threshold ($p_{\text{GHZ}} \approx 15\%$ bulk-measurement error) at $p_{\text{res}} = 10^{-3}$. Lattice surgery for logical operations maintains similar thresholds, with performance ultimately limited by the high-coherence data qubits rather than photonic communication.
